Painted around 1913 using watercolor and wash on paper, 'Journey's End' by Abanindranath Tagore is universally recognized as one of the supreme masterpieces of pathos (Karuna Rasa) in modern world art. Created around 1970 by master sculptor and printmaker Somnath Hore, 'Children' from the celebrated 'Wounds' series is one of the most heartbreaking and ethically uncompromising humanist statements in modern world art. Hore's artistic consciousness was indelibly shaped by his firsthand witness of human agony during the man-made 1943 Bengal Famine and the 1946 Tebhaga peasant uprising. Created around 1940 by master artist Jamini Roy, 'Mother and Child' is a seminal monument of modern Indian folk revivalism. Trained initially in British academic realism and having experimented with the Bengal wash style, Roy made a radical break around 1921 to return to the living folk craft traditions of his native Bankura district in rural Bengal. Drawing inspiration from Kalighat scroll paintings (patuas) and village terracotta toys, Roy eliminated academic photographic shading and perspective. In 'Mother and Child', the mother tenderly cradles her infant in a sweeping protective embrace. Both figures are rendered with bold, fluid, unbroken black contour lines and oversized, expressive almond-shaped eyes that dominate their serene faces. Roy rejected expensive imported oil paints, grinding his own natural pigments from alluvial river clay, turmeric, chalk, and soot mixed with tree gum, creating a flat, democratic, and universally accessible art form, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), New Delhi.
